$comment:
Attestation-verifier conformance corpus, v0 (S051 ③, SDK side).

WHAT THIS PINS.
Core produces an attestation about what is on a disk; the two SDKs verify it and
nothing else. This corpus is the single place where "verified" is defined, and
both implementations read it:

  python/tests/test_attest_verify_corpus.py
  node/tests/attestVerifyCorpus.test.ts

Each case carries the whole verdict -- every check identifier, its outcome, and
its detail sentence -- so the two SDKs cannot drift into describing the same
attestation differently. A customer who runs the Python verifier and a customer
who runs the Node one must be told the same thing about the same bytes.

EVERY CHECK HAS A PAIR.
A test suite built only from broken material is passed by an implementation that
answers red to everything, and a suite built only from healthy material is
passed by one that answers green. Cross-review caught exactly that on the Core
side of this sprint. So each check appears at least twice: in a case that must
reject, and in a case that must accept. `healthy-full-green` is the control
where all fifteen checks pass; `silence-same-head-again` is the control where
fourteen pass and the one that matters fails.

`must` IS THE SPECIFICATION; `expected` IS THE PIN.
`must` (which checks have to fail, pass and skip) is written by hand from the
contract. `expected` is generated, and the generator refuses to emit a case
whose generated verdict disagrees with its hand-written `must`. Without that,
the corpus would only record whatever the implementation already did -- green
forever, and proving nothing.

SKIP IS NOT PASS.
Several cases exist purely to pin that a check which could not run says so:
`healthy-first-observation` (no baseline yet, so silence is not yet ruled out),
`inventory-not-supplied-is-not-inventory-checked` (contract section 6 -- Core
holds no expected inventory, so an SDK that reported "inventory OK" would be
claiming a property nobody established), and every malformed document, where
there is nothing to verify a signature over. S012 is the reason this is pinned
rather than assumed: a shipped verifier answered LEDGER OK and exit 0 about
evidence that did not exist.

PROVENANCE IS RECORDED PER CASE.
  core-binary        Produced AND signed by the shipped aegis-gateway binary
                     (ed25519-dalek) on branch s051/autonomy-postcondition.
                     These are what prove the SDK rebuilds the canonical message
                     byte for byte -- including the 8-byte little-endian length
                     prefix over UTF-8 BYTES, which a capsule id outside ASCII
                     is what catches.
  synthetic-openssl  Signed with node:crypto (OpenSSL) using the same published
                     test seed, for the shapes the binary cannot be made to
                     produce on demand -- a fully clean attestation needs a live
                     audit ledger, and a forgery needs a signer willing to sign
                     one. The signatures are real; only the material is staged.

THE CASES THAT CAME OUT OF READING THE CONTRACT.
`records_checked`, `first_break` and `skipped_non_capsule` were outside the
canonical message in the first draft. None of the three could manufacture false
safety -- `judged` and the findings digest were already signed -- but
`skipped_non_capsule` is the only window onto what was NOT counted, and blanking
it hid "nineteen files under the root were skipped" while verification still
succeeded. This verifier reported that during section 8.2 and Core moved all
three inside the message; the three `*-rewritten-after-signing` cases pin that
each one now breaks the signature on its own.

`key-id-is-outside-the-signature` is the mirror image: a limit, pinned so it
cannot quietly turn into a claim. `signature.key_id` is still outside the
message, so an attacker rewriting a document can set the label to whatever is
expected. Pinning it catches a rotation that moved the key without the label. It
catches nothing else, and the case exists so nobody later describes it as a
security check.

NUMBERS BOTH LANGUAGES RENDER THE SAME.
Counts above 2**53-1 are refused by both SDKs, because JavaScript cannot tell
one such integer from the next after JSON.parse and would render a different
decimal into the canonical message than the one Core signed. That is a stated
limit, not a silent one, and `malformed-sequence-beyond-exact-integers` pins it.

chain_status_meaning.valid: The walk completed and every record in the inspected range linked and rehashed correctly. An EMPTY ledger is valid — a genuine zero-record chain; records_checked is how a caller tells that apart.
chain_status_meaning.broken: The walk found an inconsistency; first_break names the first one.
chain_status_meaning.absent: The ledger file does not exist. Explicitly NOT a verdict about integrity — a statement that there was nothing to walk.
chain_status_meaning.not-checked: No ledger path was supplied to attest. The chain half of the report was never attempted.
chain_status_meaning.unreadable: The walk itself failed — the path exists but could not be traversed; first_break carries the error.

pinned.note: A published test key. The seed is in the corpus on purpose: these vectors have to be regenerable, and a key whose private half is printed here can never be mistaken for a deployment key.

unexpected.note: The attacker-with-a-key case: valid signatures, wrong signer.

cases.doc: THE RESIDUAL, not a limit any more. Contract §4: an EMPTY ledger is `valid` — a genuine zero-record chain — so this document (three capsules, a ledger that has never recorded anything) is structurally sound and this verifier has NO independent check for it. It verifies clean here only because `abnormal` is empty. Core now reports the state itself, so a real attestation of this shape carries an abnormal line and `core_abnormal` fails — see `empty-ledger-core-reports-it`. What this case pins is the dependency: the SDK is relying on Core's verdict, not on a check of its own, and if Core ever stopped reporting it nothing here would notice.

cases.doc: The other half. Core decided that capsules existing while the ledger has never recorded anything is abnormal — a boundary that does not hold a record of its own activity — and puts it in `abnormal` rather than moving `chain.status` off `valid`, because an empty chain really is a valid zero-record chain and changing the status would change what `valid` means for every other caller. So `chain_status` PASSES and `core_abnormal` FAILS, and that pair is what proves the finding was carried in the verdict rather than smuggled into the status.

This is also how Core's relocation cap reaches this verifier — a capsule relocated past the cap gets an `issue`, and an issue increments `inconsistent`.

cases.doc: THE LIMIT THIS VERIFIER DOES NOT OVERCLAIM. signature.key_id is the one field an operator reads that the canonical message does not cover. Here the producer labelled the attestation 's051-rotated' and the label was rewritten in flight to 's051-demo', which is what the deployment pins — and signing_key PASSES. The key itself is what authenticates, so nothing is actually forged; pinning key_id catches a rotation that moved the key without the label, and catches nothing an attacker does. Pinned as a case so the limit cannot be quietly forgotten and later described as a check.

cases.doc: Produced and signed by the shipped aegis-gateway binary (ed25519-dalek) on branch s051/autonomy-postcondition. This is the vector that proves the SDK rebuilds the canonical message byte for byte rather than plausibly — it carries a real loss, a real inconsistency, a terminal capsule, a null payload_bytes, an absolute path inside an issue string and a capsule id outside ASCII. The attestation is abnormal (Core said so) and the SIGNATURE is what must verify.
